newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ghana's Kofi Annan sworn in as new U.N. chief.
newsitem.headline: Ghana's Kofi Annan sworn in as new U.N. chief.

text.p: Kofi Annan, a 58-year-old U.N. career official from Ghana, was sworn in on Tuesday for a five-year term as secretary-general of the United Nations, beginning January 1, 1997.

"As a son of Africa and as a lifetime international civil servant I pledge to you that I will do everything in my power to be worthy of your trust," he said after being appointed by acclamation by the 185-nation General Assembly and taking the oath of office from Assembly President Razali Ismail of Malaysia.

"If all of us in this hall together, with the participation of nations large and small, East and West, North and South, can make this organisation leaner, more efficient and more effective, more responsive to the wishes and needs of its members and more realistic in its goal and commitments, then and only then will we serve both this organisation's high purpose and the planet's best interest."
The grey-bearded Annan, currently undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations, will be the seventh secretary-general in U.N. history.
He will also be the first from sub-Saharan Africa and the first to have risen through the ranks of the U.N. bureaucracy.
The 15-member Security Council nominated him to the $205,809-a-year post last Friday, making his appointment by the Assembly a formality.
He succeeds the 74-year-old Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, to whom the Assembly paid tribute in another resolution adopted by acclamation.
The United States blocked his hopes for a second term by vetoing his candidacy last month, saying he had not done enough to carry out reforms and that the world organisation needed new leadership.
Razali, as well as a number of other diplomats, added splashes of colour to the ceremony by wearing national dress.

Annan, wearing a grey business suit and red patterned tie, called in his address for "a healing of fractures and frictions between member states and this organisation...a healing of wounded morale and ideals within the (U.N.) secretariat."

"To the nations and peoples of the world whose representatives are assembled here, I say simply this: the United Nations is your instrument for peace and justice. Use it; respect it; defend it. It can be no more competent and no more efficient than those member states that now comprise and guide it."

Annan also praised the "vision and energy" of Boutros-Ghali, switching to French during part of his speech to display the fluency that France has made a requirement for anyone aspiring to the top U.N. post.

Boutros-Ghali's predecessor as secretary-general, Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, was among those attending the gala ceremony in the gold and blue Assembly hall. So was Annan's Swedish artist wife, Nane, and Boutros-Ghali's wife, Leia.

Security Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy and representatives of the five main U.N. regional groups hailed the incoming secretary-general and paid tribute to the departing U.N. chief. So did ambassador Madeleine Albright, soon to become U.S. Secretary of State, on behalf of the U.N.'s host country.

Boutros-Ghali, in a farewell address, delivered a thinly-veiled jab at the United States for arrears to the world body totalling some $1.3 billion and stressed the need for a secretary-general to be totally independent.
The U.N. financial crisis was "not the result of mismanagement," he said, rejecting an oft-levelled charge.

"It is the refusal to fulfil a treaty obligation. Now that a new secretary-general is being appointed, all arrears should be paid at once, as has been promised so often in the past few months," he said pointedly. Albright, seated at the head of her delegation, looked on stonily.

Boutros-Ghali, speaking in English, French and Arabic, said that during his five-year term, coinciding with the end of the Cold War, the United Nations passed through periods of enthusiasm, disillusion and realism.

"Now let us look to the future," he said. "The holder of this office must never be seen as acting out of fear of, or in an attempt to curry favour with, one state or group of states. Should that happen, all prospects for the United Nations would be lost."
